# Chapter 4: The 2 A.M. Problem

You put her down at seven-thirty. She went down easily, maybe after one extra song. You ate dinner while it was still warm, watched half an episode of something, and went to bed feeling like a functioning adult. Then, at 2:14, the monitor crackled. By 2:20 you were standing in a dark hallway negotiating with a two-year-old about whether the blue cup or the green cup was the correct cup for water she didn't actually want.

If that sounds familiar, this chapter is for you. Bedtime gets most of the attention in sleep advice, but for many families the real battle happens in the middle of the night. The good news is that night waking in toddlers usually follows a pattern, and patterns can be changed.

## Why Toddlers Wake Up at Night

Everybody wakes up at night. Adults surface briefly between sleep cycles several times, roll over, pull the blanket up, and drift off again without remembering any of it. Toddlers do the same thing. The difference is what they find when they surface.

If your child fell asleep while being rocked, fed, or lying next to you, she wakes at 2 a.m. into a situation that has changed. The arms are gone. The bottle is gone. You are gone. From her point of view, this is a bit like falling asleep in your bed and waking up on the kitchen floor. Of course she calls for help.

This is why the single most important night-waking fix actually happens at bedtime. A child who falls asleep on her own, in her own bed, in the same conditions she'll find later, has far less reason to call out when she stirs.

Other common causes are worth ruling out before you change anything:

- **Hunger.** Most toddlers over 12 months don't need calories overnight, but a child who ate very little at dinner may genuinely wake hungry. Look at the whole day's intake, not just the evening.
- **Discomfort.** Teething molars, a stuffy nose, a wet diaper, a room that's too warm. If the waking is new and sudden, check the body first.
- **Too much daytime sleep, or too little.** A nap that runs late into the afternoon can push the whole night later. A skipped nap can leave a child so overtired that her sleep becomes fragmented.
- **Developmental leaps.** Language explosions, learning to climb, starting daycare. Big changes often show up at night for a week or two.

## The Consistent Response

Once you've ruled out a physical cause, the goal is to make night wakings as boring as possible. Not cruel, not cold. Boring.

Decide in advance, ideally with your partner over coffee and not at 2 a.m., what you will do when she wakes. Then do exactly that, every time, for at least two weeks. Toddlers will test whether Tuesday's rule still applies on Thursday.

A simple version looks like this:

1. Wait a few minutes before going in. Many children grumble and resettle on their own if given the chance.
2. If she's still calling, go in calmly. Keep the lights off or very low.
3. Offer a brief, predictable phrase. Something like, "It's still sleeping time. I love you. Goodnight." Use the same words every night.
4. Lay her back down, tuck the blanket, and leave.
5. If she calls again, repeat, with the same words and the same short visit.

No new snacks, no trips to the living room, no long conversations about the dog. Each of those is interesting, and interesting is the enemy.

## The "Sleep Pass" and Other Tools for Older Toddlers

Children closer to three can understand simple systems. One family I worked with used a laminated card they called the "night ticket." Their son got one ticket per night. He could trade it for one visit from a parent, for any reason. Once the ticket was used, it was used. If he still had it in the morning, he could trade it for a small reward at breakfast. Within ten days he was hanging on to his ticket almost every night, mostly because he liked choosing a sticker.
## What to Expect in the First Week

Here is the honest part. When you change your response, night waking usually gets worse before it gets better. Your child is not being manipulative; she's confused, and she's checking whether the old system still works. Nights two through four are often the hardest. Most families see a clear improvement by the end of the first week and a mostly settled pattern by the end of the second.

Write things down. A simple log of when she woke, how long it lasted, and what you did will show you progress you might miss when you're exhausted. A night with two short wakings instead of four long ones is a win, even if it doesn't feel like one at 3 a.m.

And look after yourself while you're in the thick of it. Take turns with your partner if you can. Go to bed earlier than feels reasonable. This phase is temporary, and the steadier you are, the faster it passes.

In the next chapter, we'll look at early rising, the 5 a.m. wake-up that so many parents assume they simply have to live with.
